route_summary: Open. Two blind attempts from one cycle: 001 relaxed the counterexample conditions to a reciprocal-sum problem and certified more than 3355 prime factors and 10^10395, with an explicit witness capping that whole family at 8135; 002 established that a counterexample is too large to be an object and went after the ones that are not -- odd Giuga numbers (none below 12 prime factors, and the count must be even) and Giuga sequences (complete to length 6). Read 001 for the bound, 002 for the objects and the closed forms that make any Giuga enumeration cheap.

attempts.one_line: Relaxing the counterexample conditions to 'odd primes, none dividing another minus one, reciprocals summing above 1' yields a searchable bound of more than 3355 prime factors and 10^10395, plus an explicit 8135-prime set proving the relaxation can never exceed 8135.
attempts.range: Congruence formulations cross-checked for n = 2..4000 (Agoh's form to 261); Giuga numbers enumerated exhaustively to 7 prime factors (8 factors aborts, needing candidate primes to 5.4e10); factor bound at branch limit X = 701 over the odd primes below 3e6; size bound at X = 307; ceiling witness of 8135 primes checked over all 66,170,090 ordered pairs.
gaps: The bound is about a relaxation: it drops the exact Giuga divisibility conditions, so a large admissible set is not a near-counterexample.
L(X) for X > 73 rests on one search program; only the winning leaf is re-verified exactly, not the claim that no other configuration is smaller.
Exhaustiveness of the 6- and 7-factor Giuga lists rests on one enumerator, validated by toggling its pruning rules rather than by a second program.
Cost grows 4-5x per step of the branch limit (18s, 70s, 336s at X = 503, 601, 701), so the ceiling of 8135 is unreachable in pure Python.
attempts.note: target_shape is mixed: the deliverable was a lower bound (proof-shaped), but the most durable artifact was the 8135-prime ceiling witness, which is an object a checker settles. The two pushes past the first partial result were the product/digit objective and the explicit ceiling construction. Fields added after the record was written, when the schema gained them; the record prose is unchanged.

attempts.one_line: A Giuga counterexample is object-shaped but provably enormous, so this went after the nearby objects that are not: no odd Giuga number below 12 prime factors, its factor count must be even, Giuga sequences complete to length 6, and a closed form (ap-N)(aq-N) = N^2-a that replaces the last-two-primes scan.
attempts.range: Odd Giuga numbers exhausted at 9, 10, 11 prime factors and odd Giuga sequences at lengths 7-11, with no unresolved branches; Giuga sequences complete for lengths 3-6; the parity law proved for m <= 1411, where k = 1 is forced; the construction search settled 1,059,471,340 window integers across 1,099,847 prefixes at factor counts 3 to 61 on one seed, finding nothing.
gaps: Nothing is claimed about whether an odd Giuga number exists; the construction search samples a vanishing fraction of prefixes.
Exhaustiveness beyond length 11 depends on N^2 - a factoring; branches that resist are reported but not resolved.
The parity law only bites while k = 1, i.e. m <= 1411; beyond that odd factor counts are not excluded.
Odd lengths 9 and 11 were searched before the parity law was found, and are vacuous -- the only real exclusion in that range is length 10.
The 8-prime-factor Giuga list and odd sequences of length 12 both did not finish; measured costs are in the record, and neither is reported as evidence of absence.
attempts.methodological_lesson: Two rounds of compute went into odd factor counts that a two-line parity argument excludes for free. When a search comes back empty at several consecutive sizes, look for a reason those sizes are vacuous before paying for the next one.
